criterion_notes.c1: Fails C1: Rather than household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access, the paper empirically examines watershed-scale land-cover change, bulk raw-water extraction concessions (CONAGUA/REPDA groundwater and surface-water permits across agricultural vs. municipal/domestic public uses), municipal income inequality/marginalization, and health morbidity/mortality. Statements about household water/sanitation deficits (e.g., 56% lacking basic water services in Chiapas, lack of sewerage/wastewater treatment in two municipalities, shared latrines) are cited only as secondary background from CONEVAL (2020) and Alvarado Velázquez et al. (2022).
criterion_notes.c2: Fails C2 under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording (and would still be excluded even if a very broad plain reading counted descriptive REPDA water-rights concession counts). Narrow 2026-10-13 reading: No rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or institutional mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure rules, tariffs, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure) is empirically examined; CONAGUA's centralized urban prioritization (>2,500 inhabitants), APARURAL, informal ejidal water practices, and SDG 16 governance appear only in the Discussion as unanalysed institutional background and normative 'levers for action'. Plain reading: Governance (SDG 16) is explicitly framed as a conceptual Discussion lever rather than an empirical variable in Methods/Results, where the study's drivers are agricultural land-cover intensification and income inequality and REPDA water-rights concessions are merely tallied descriptively by water source and sector; even if descriptive water-rights data were viewed as touching broadly on a legal instrument, no governance exposure is linked to household or community service access, so plain_criterion2_decision remains exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Meets C3: Contains quantitative and spatial empirical analyses of official secondary datasets across three municipalities in Chiapas (INEGI land-use/vegetation maps 2002-2017; REPDA water-concession registry 1994-2019; DGEPI/SINAVE morbidity 1998-2018 including local polynomial regressions; INEGI mortality records 1998-2019; and INEGI/CONAPO Palma ratio and Marginalization Index).
criterion_notes.c4: Fails C4: Reports municipal land-cover change, counts and volume shares of bulk watershed extraction concessions (agricultural vs. municipal/domestic public use), gastrointestinal morbidity trends, pesticide/cancer-related mortality trends, and socioeconomic inequality/marginalization indices. It does not report empirical outcomes of household or community water or sanitation service access, connection, continuity, reliability, affordability, or household exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Meets C5 for the paper's own empirical scope: The municipal unit of analysis (three municipalities in the RGCLM watershed), environmental/socioeconomic drivers, sectoral concession/health indicators, and ecological multi-municipality case-study design are identifiable (note p. 4 contains an obvious typo '295 persons' for ~295 thousand inhabitants, whereas p. 7 gives the exact municipal populations: 166,178, 83,111, and 46,409). However, no legal/governance exposure to household service-access outcome is operationalized.
criterion_notes.c6: Meets C6: Full text is published in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: Drawing on the case study of three municipalities in the Río Grande de Comitán-Lagos de Montebello watershed in Chiapas, Mexico, we illustrate some of the consequences of the intensification of agricultural activities, alongside urban expansion, at the expense of forests and the negative impact on the water quality of surrounding areas during the last two decades.

We discuss how individual and collective action (SDG 11), economy and finance (SDG 12), and governance (SDG 16) can act as levers for action to halt environmental degradation and its associated negative impacts on human health.

Following our conceptual framework (Fig. 1), we examined the indirect potential consequences to human health of unequal access to clean water and exposure to environmental degradation. Thus, we developed a set of analyses to assess whether there was environmental degradation or not in the study area, in terms of land/cover change in general, and more specifically, in relation with the intensification of agricultural activities and its impacts on water provision and contamination.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 6 (SDG 6: water concessions and uses)
evidence_quotes.quote: We wanted to explore whether there was a potential relation between the type of use and the water rights to obtain water in the RGCLM watershed in the three municipalities under study. Thus, we produced a qualitative, spatially explicit representation of the link between water uses and water concessions in the watershed.
By type of use, agricultural activities comprise the main users (1083 concessions) in the RGCLM watershed, followed by concessions for municipal and domestic public use (192 concessions).

raw_response.exposure: Intensification of agricultural activities and urban expansion / land-cover change (2002–2017) and municipal income inequality and marginalization (Palma ratio 2000–2010; CONAPO Marginalization Index 2015–2020)
raw_response.outcome: Watershed land-cover change, counts and volume shares of bulk water-extraction concessions (REPDA 1994–2019 across groundwater/surface water and agricultural vs. domestic public uses), municipal prevalence of gastrointestinal diseases (1998–2018), and mortality from causes potentially associated with pesticides including cancer (1998–2019)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Three municipalities in the Río Grande de Comitán-Lagos de Montebello watershed, Chiapas, Mexico: Comitán de Domínguez (166,178 inhabitants), La Trinitaria (83,111 inhabitants), and La Independencia (46,409 inhabitants)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; also lacks a qualifying C2 governance exposure and C4 household/community service-access outcome). Although titled around 'water accessibility', this ecological SDG-interlinkages study empirically analyzes watershed land-cover change (agricultural intensification and deforestation), bulk raw-water extraction concessions from CONAGUA's REPDA registry (groundwater vs. surface water; agricultural vs. municipal/domestic public abstraction permits), municipal income inequality and marginalization, and epidemiological morbidity/mortality (gastrointestinal diseases and cancer deaths) across three municipalities in Chiapas. Household water and sanitation service conditions are cited only from secondary literature, and governance (SDG 16), CONAGUA's centralized concession framework, and local community practices appear only as unanalysed background context and normative policy 'levers for action' in the Discussion rather than an empirically tested mechanism governing household or community service access.
raw_response.study_design: Ecological multi-municipality case study using secondary spatial, administrative, epidemiological, and census datasets
